newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court allows alien deportation for fraud.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court allows alien deportation for fraud.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court said Wednesday the Immigration and Naturalisation Service might consider an alien's acts of fraud in entering the United States when deciding whether to proceed with deportation.

The high court ruled in a seven-page opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia that the law at issue imposed no limits on the factors that might be taken into account in determining whether to grant an alien a waiver of deportation.

The case involved a man identified as Yueh-shaio Yang and his wife, who were born in China and moved to Taiwan in 1945. The scheme involved the wife's divorcing her husband in Taiwan and coming to the United States in 1978 to obtain a fraudulent birth certificate and passport in the name of a U.S. citizen.

She then remarried her husband in Taiwan under her false identity and obtained an immigration visa for him to enter the United States as the spouse of a U.S. citizen. While his request for U.S. citizenship was pending, his wife decided to abandon her false identity and the immigration agency eventually learned of the fradulent scheme.
At the time of his deportation proceeding in 1992, Yang had substantial assets, including more than $3 million in property, real estate, cash and stocks.

Yang conceded he was deportable but requested a waiver. A board of immigration appeals denied the request. It did not consider his fradulent entry into the country but did take into account his other actions, including his sham divorce.

Scalia said the immigration agency had broad discretion in its decisions and might distinguish between those like Yang who engaged in a pattern of immigration fraud and those who committed a single isolated act of misrepresentation.
